It showcases the practical value of AI tools in accelerating knowledge translation, parameter generation, and issue localization for cross-cloud network configuration. Table of Contents 01 1. Introduction: Engineering challenges of cross-cloud interconnectivity As multi-cloud strategies become increasingly prevalent, cross-cloud private network interconnectivity has become a common enterprise infrastructure requirement. A typical scenario: business teams have deployed services on both AWS and Tencent Cloud, and need the VPCs on both sides to communicate over the intranet via IPSec VPN, while meeting high-availability requirements for dual-tunnel redundancy and automatic failover. This requirement is not technically novel, but the engineering complexity is considerable: The VPN product models, API styles, and parameter naming conventions of the two cloud platforms differ significantly IKE/IPSec negotiation parameters must strictly match on both sides; any mismatch will cause tunnel negotiation to fail There are three routing modes on the Tencent Cloud side (SPD policy routing, destination routing, BGP dynamic routing), and the selection directly determines the failover mechanism The orchestration involves multiple resources including VPN gateways, customer gateways, VPN tunnels, route tables, and security groups For an engineer familiar with AWS but with no prior exposure to the Tencent Cloud CLI (tccli), the traditional approach requires constantly switching between documentation, consoles, and terminals on both sides, and building and tuning a complete dual-tunnel solution typically takes 1-2 days. This article shows how two AI tools collaborate with a division of labor: Claude Code handles the Tencent Cloud side, while Kiro CLI handles the AWS side, completing iterative builds of three architecture approaches within one day. You will see: The evolution logic and applicable scenarios of the three architecture approaches (SPD, VPC destination routing, CCN destination routing) Six key technical decision points for cross-cloud IPSec VPN setup How AI tools accelerate learning of unfamiliar cloud platforms and multi-resource orchestration Quantitative efficiency comparison of the setup process 2. Tool introduction: Claude Code and Kiro CLI Before diving into the solution setup, let me introduce the two AI tools used in this article, and why they are well-suited for complex tasks like cross-cloud network construction. 2.1 Claude Code: AI development assistant in the terminal Claude Code is a command-line AI assistant launched by Anthropic that runs in the terminal and can: Understand requirements through natural language dialogue, generating and executing Shell commands Read and write local files, handling configuration files such as JSON/YAML Maintain multi-turn conversation context, making it suitable for progressive exploration and learning In this article's scenario, Claude Code handled all work on the Tencent Cloud side: learning the tccli command system, generating creation commands for VPN gateways and tunnels, writing JSON output parsing scripts, and explaining the conceptual differences between SPD and destination routing. Its core value lies in "translating" the existing network knowledge of AWS engineers into the Tencent Cloud API system. 2.2 Kiro CLI: AWS-native AI operations tool Kiro is an AI-driven development environment launched by AWS, offered in both IDE and CLI forms. Kiro CLI runs in the terminal and can connect to AWS services via MCP (Model Context Protocol) to directly operate AWS resources. In this article's scenario, Kiro CLI handled all work on the AWS side: VGW creation, Customer Gateway configuration, VPN Connection tunnel parameter generation, route propagation settings, and security group configuration. 2.3 Division of labor model The two tools use a "each side managed by one tool" division of labor: Responsibility Tool Specific content Tencent Cloud side configuration Claude Code VPN gateway, customer gateway, VPN tunnel, VPN gateway route table, VPC route table AWS side configuration Kiro CLI VGW, Customer Gateway, VPN Connection, route propagation, security groups Architecture decisions and parameter alignment Engineer IKE/IPSec parameter matching, routing mode selection, subnet planning The core advantage of this division: each tool only maintains context for its own side, avoiding cross-platform conceptual confusion. However, parameter alignment between the two sides (encryption algorithms, DH groups, SA lifetimes, etc.) must be done manually by the engineer — the AI does not know what the other side is configured with. 3. Two-cloud environment and network planning 3.1 Network topology [Figure 1] 3.2 Tunnel parameter planning Parameter Tunnel 1 Tunnel 2 Inside CIDR 169.254.200.0/30 169.254.201.0/30 IKE version IKEv2 IKEv2 IKE encryption AES-CBC-128 AES-CBC-128 IKE authentication SHA1 SHA1 DH group GROUP2 GROUP2 IPSec encryption AES-CBC-128 AES-CBC-128 IPSec authentication SHA1 SHA1 PFS DH-GROUP2 DH-GROUP2 IKE SA lifetime 28800 seconds 28800 seconds IPSec SA lifetime 3600 seconds 3600 seconds Key constraint: The above parameters must strictly match on both sides. AWS and Tencent Cloud have different defaults, so each item must be manually aligned one by one. 4. Evolution of three architecture approaches During the setup process we iterated through three approaches. Each iteration stemmed from real pain points of the previous approach, not from advance planning. AI tools made this "discover problem — research alternatives — reimplement" loop fast enough to complete three rounds within a single day. 4.1 Approach 1: SPD policy routing Core idea: Configure SPD (Security Policy Database) rules on each VPN tunnel, specifying the traffic range carried by that tunnel. Tunnel 1 SPD: 172.16.0.0/24 ↔ 172.31.99.0/25 ← real business traffic Tunnel 2 SPD: 10.255.0.0/24 ↔ 10.255.1.0/24 ← placeholder (carries no traffic) Why Tunnel 2 needs a placeholder subnet: Tencent Cloud's API prohibits SPD subnet pairs of different tunnels under the same VPN gateway from overlapping. SPD is a flat matching table with no priority field — two rules matching the same packet constitutes a conflict. Therefore, Tunnel 2 must be filled with a placeholder subnet that will never carry real traffic. Failover mechanism: A external script (failover.sh) polls Tunnel 1 status every 30 seconds and, upon failure, calls the API to swap the SPD rules of the two tunnels. Assessment: The approach is workable, but operationally heavy — it requires maintaining a resident script, failover is slow, and the placeholder subnet adds configuration obscurity. 4.2 Approach 2: VPC type + destination routing Core improvement: Create the VPN tunnel without the SecurityPolicyDatabases parameter, entering destination routing mode. Traffic matching moves from tunnel-level SPD rules to the VPN gateway's route table. VPN gateway route table (independent of tunnels): 172.31.0.0/16 → Tunnel 1, priority 0 ← primary (highest priority) 172.31.0.0/16 → Tunnel 2, priority 100 ← standby Failover mechanism: DPD (Dead Peer Detection) + NQA health checks probe the tunnel internal IP. The platform performs failover automatically, with no scripts required. Assessment: Significantly better than Approach 1. No script dependency, and both tunnel configurations are fully symmetric. The VPC route table still requires manually adding a 172.31.0.0/16 - VPN GW entry. 4.3 Approach 3: CCN cloud networking + destination routing Core improvement: The VPN gateway type changes from IPSEC (bound to a single VPC) to CCN (bound to a cloud networking instance). Both the VPC and VPN gateway are attached to CCN, and routes propagate automatically — no need to manually add entries in the VPC route table. Failover mechanism: Identical to Approach 2 (health checks + route priority). Assessment: Best scalability. New VPCs can simply be attached to CCN, and routes propagate automatically. The trade-offs are the additional cost of CCN, and the fact that the VPN gateway type cannot be changed after creation. 4.4 Core comparison of the three approaches Dimension SPD policy routing VPC + destination routing CCN + destination routing VPN gateway type IPSEC (VPC type) IPSEC (VPC type) CCN type Traffic matching location Per-tunnel (SPD) VPN gateway route table VPN gateway route table Tunnel 2 configuration Placeholder subnet Real subnet + priority Real subnet + priority Failover Script swaps SPD Platform automatic Platform automatic VPC route management Manual addition Manual addition CCN automatic propagation Scalability Single VPC Single VPC Multi-VPC / multi-region Additional cost None None CCN fees Suitable scenarios Temporary testing Single-VPC environments Multi-VPC interconnectivity One-sentence summary: the complexity of Approach 1 lies in the operations script, Approach 2 eliminates the script dependency, and Approach 3 further eliminates manual route management. The AWS-side configuration is identical across all three approaches — the differences are entirely on the Tencent Cloud side. 5. Key technical decision points The following six technical points are the most error-prone aspects of cross-cloud IPSec setup. Each one is not difficult to solve on its own, but if you are not aware of it in advance, it can add several extra hours of troubleshooting. 5.1 Strict IKE/IPSec parameter matching AWS and Tencent Cloud have different default encryption parameters. If any one of the encryption algorithm, authentication algorithm, DH group, or SA lifetime mismatches between the two sides, the tunnel will show as "established" but traffic will not pass. Regarding IKE versions, both IKEv1 and IKEv2 work (IKEv2 is recommended; IKEv1 has been deprecated by the IETF), with the key point being that both sides must match. Recommendation: Create a parameter comparison table before starting, fill in the values for both sides item by item, and confirm they are fully consistent before proceeding. 5.2 The 169.254.128.0/17 restriction for Inside CIDR AWS requires that the tunnel internal IP must be within the 169.254.128.0/17 range. If a CIDR outside this range is specified when creating the VPN Connection, subsequent health checks will fail to probe successfully. This restriction is documented in the AWS documentation but is not prominently highlighted. 5.3 VPN gateway type lock-in Tencent Cloud's VPN gateway requires selecting a type at creation time: IPSEC (bound to a VPC) or CCN (bound to cloud networking). This cannot be changed after creation. If you chose the IPSEC type and later need to switch to CCN, you can only delete and recreate — the public IP will change, and the Customer Gateway on the AWS side must also be updated accordingly. Recommendation: If there is any possibility of multi-VPC interconnectivity, choose the CCN type directly. 5.4 Tencent Cloud API parameter typo The integrity algorithm parameter in the IPSec configuration is named IntegrityAlgorith (missing the final m). This is not a documentation typo — the API genuinely requires this spelling. If you pass the correctly spelled IntegrityAlgorithm, the field is ignored and the default value is used, causing negotiation failure due to mismatch with the AWS side. 5.5 Static routing vs BGP selection Tencent Cloud's BGP feature requires submitting a ticket for approval, with a review cycle of 1-3 business days. For a scenario of two fixed VPCs interconnecting, static routing + destination routing is sufficient. The advantages of BGP are seen in scenarios such as multiple peer gateways, frequently changing subnets, and the need for ECMP load balancing. Additionally, the routing mode selections on the two sides are independent — using Static on AWS and destination routing on Tencent Cloud is perfectly viable. 5.6 Health checks use tunnel internal IP The NQA health check probes the tunnel's Inside IP (e.g., 169.254.200.1), not the business IP inside the VPC. When creating the tunnel, HealthCheckLocalIp (Tencent Cloud side, the second IP address in the /30 mask) and HealthCheckRemoteIp (AWS side, the first IP address in the /30 mask) must be correctly configured, and they must correspond to addresses within the Inside CIDR. 6. Real interactions during AI-assisted setup The following shows typical interaction scenarios with AI tools during the setup process. 6.1 Scenario 1: Using Claude Code to learn the tccli command system User: I create a VGW on AWS using aws ec2 create-vpn-gateway. What is the corresponding Tencent Cloud command? Claude Code: The corresponding Tencent Cloud command is tccli vpc CreateVpnGateway. Note a few key differences: - Parameters use PascalCase: --VpnGatewayName instead of --tag-specifications - The region code differs: na-ashburn (not us-east-1) - You must specify a type: --Type IPSEC (VPC-bound type) or --Type CCN (cloud networking type) Full command: tccli vpc CreateVpnGateway --region na-ashburn \ --VpcId vpc-74e8d5oj \ --VpnGatewayName ipsec-to-aws-demo \ --InternetMaxBandwidthOut 200 \ --InstanceChargeType POSTPAID_BY_HOUR \ --Type IPSEC \ --output json 6.2 Scenario 2: Claude Code generates complex JSON parameters User: Help me generate the command to create a VPN tunnel — no SPD, destination routing mode, health check enabled, and IKE and IPSec parameters matching the AWS side. Claude Code: The key to destination routing mode: do not pass the SecurityPolicyDatabases parameter. Also enable EnableHealthCheck, using IPs from the Inside CIDR. tccli vpc CreateVpnConnection --region na-ashburn \ --VpnGatewayId vpngw-duvztsy6 \ --CustomerGatewayId cgw-w0dfsygg \ --VpnConnectionName ipsec-to-aws-tunnel1 \ --PreShareKey \"uluplyRaPEMsmN.aYVagRdq6PAiLxB_C\" \ --IKEOptionsSpecification '{...14 fields...}' \ --IPSECOptionsSpecification '{ \"EncryptAlgorithm\": \"AES-CBC-128\", \"IntegrityAlgorith\": \"SHA1\", ← Note: this is how the API spells it ... }' \ --EnableHealthCheck true \ --HealthCheckLocalIp \"169.254.200.2\" \ --HealthCheckRemoteIp \"169.254.200.1\" \ --output json Note: IntegrityAlgorith is missing the final m — this is a known API spelling quirk, and you must pass it exactly this way. 6.3 Scenario 3: Kiro CLI configures the AWS-side VPN Connection User: Create a VPN Connection to Tencent Cloud in us-east-1, static routing mode. The public IP of the Tencent Cloud VPN gateway is 43.166.166.238, and I have already planned the Inside CIDRs and PSKs for the two tunnels. Kiro: OK, I'll create the Customer Gateway and VPN Connection. Executing command: aws ec2 create-customer-gateway \ --type ipsec.1 --bgp-asn 65001 \ --ip-address 43.166.166.238 --region us-east-1 Customer Gateway created: cgw-0ce0b5bd55dfd47e5 Executing command: aws ec2 create-vpn-connection \ --type ipsec.1 \ --customer-gateway-id cgw-0ce0b5bd55dfd47e5 \ --vpn-gateway-id vgw-0ba7d31bccaba979c \ --options '{\"StaticRoutesOnly\": true, \"TunnelOptions\": [...]}' VPN Connection created: vpn-0bbb0ef3bc912cbf9 Tunnel 1 public IP: 52.23.132.149 Tunnel 2 public IP: 54.88.240.175 Next step: provide these two IPs to the Tencent Cloud side for creating the customer gateway. 6.4 Scenario 4: Claude Code parses tccli JSON output User: tccli's output is plain JSON, unlike aws cli which has --query. Help me write a quick command to check tunnel status. Claude Code: tccli indeed has no JMESPath support. Use a python3 one-liner to parse: tccli vpc DescribeVpnConnections --region na-ashburn \ --VpnConnectionIds '[\"vpnx-ls3pkmdn\",\"vpnx-zhvk9zd5\"]' \ --output json | python3 -c \" import sys, json for c in json.load(sys.stdin)['VpnConnectionSet']: print(f\\"{c['VpnConnectionName']}: {c['NetStatus']}\\") \" Expected output: ipsec-to-aws-tunnel1: AVAILABLE ipsec-to-aws-tunnel2: AVAILABLE The above conversations have been simplified and reorganized. In actual interactions, the AI tools occasionally generated outdated parameter names or omitted optional configuration, and the engineer needed to validate against documentation. 7. Quantitative efficiency comparison 7.1 Setup complexity comparison Dimension Approach 1 (SPD) Approach 2 (destination routing) Approach 3 (CCN) Tencent Cloud resources 5 7 (including VPN gateway routes) 9 (including CCN instance) AWS resources 4 4 4 Additional scripts failover.sh None None Biggest challenge SPD placeholder design VPN gateway route table configuration CCN instance association 7.2 Traditional approach vs AI-assisted efficiency comparison Dimension Traditional approach AI-assisted (Claude Code + Kiro CLI) Learning tccli command system 1-2 days (reading docs + trial and error) 2-3 hours (interactive learning) Single-approach setup time 3-5 hours 1-2 hours Three-approach iteration total time 3-5 days 1 day Parameter mismatch troubleshooting 1-2 hours (checking docs item by item) 15 minutes (AI generates comparison table) Discovering the IntegrityAlgorith spelling issue Several hours (trial and error) Immediate (AI already knows the spelling) tccli JSON output handling Writing scripts manually AI generates python3 one-liner The core efficiency gains come from three aspects: Cross-platform knowledge translation: mapping AWS concepts directly to the corresponding Tencent Cloud APIs, eliminating the need to learn from scratch Complex parameter generation: nested JSON structures like IKEOptionsSpecification are generated by AI, reducing manual typing errors Immediate issue localization: hidden problems such as API spelling errors and parameter default differences are directly identified by AI At the same time, the limitations of AI tools must be acknowledged: Parameter alignment between the two sides still requires manual work by the engineer Occasionally generates outdated API parameters, requiring validation against the latest documentation Architecture selection decisions (SPD vs destination routing vs CCN) are ultimately made by the engineer 8. Summary and approach selection recommendations 8.1 Approach selection If you... Recommended approach Only need temporary cross-cloud connectivity testing Approach 1 (SPD), fastest to get started Two fixed VPCs in production interconnectivity with automatic failover Approach 2 (VPC + destination routing) Anticipate multi-VPC / multi-region expansion needs Approach 3 (CCN + destination routing) More than 3 peer gateways, or frequently changing subnets Upgrade to BGP on top of Approach 3 8.2 Value of AI tools Regardless of the approach chosen, the Claude Code + Kiro CLI division-of-labor model significantly lowers the barrier to cross-cloud setup: Claude Code's core value: translating the existing knowledge of AWS engineers into the Tencent Cloud system, generating complex tccli commands, and identifying hidden API-level issues Kiro CLI's core value: accelerating multi-resource orchestration on the AWS side and reducing time spent looking up CLI syntax Value of the division of labor: each side being managed by one tool avoids context confusion, allowing the engineer to focus on architecture decisions and parameter alignment For multi-cloud operations engineers, AI tools do not replace professional knowledge — they amplify productivity, directing your time toward architecture decisions rather than memorizing two CLI syntaxes. 8.3 Final results Bidirectional ping succeeds with approximately 3ms latency; after Tunnel 1 fails, traffic automatically fails over to Tunnel 2. 9.
